lead: A machine part can fail in two different ways. It can break or yield when stress crosses the material strength, and it can bend or twist so much that it no longer does its job. Strength design keeps stress below an allowable value; stiffness design keeps deflection or angle of twist below a limit. Both checks use the same loads and the same trial section, but they answer different questions. Shafts, beams, brackets and machine frames are sized by running both checks and resizing until each passes.
prereq: You need 1.4 for allowable stress and 1.6 for stress formulas.

blocks.text: Strength and stiffness are separate acceptance tests. Strength asks whether the material can carry the stress without yielding or breaking. Stiffness asks whether the part deforms too much in service.

blocks.where: σmax is the largest stress in the part (MPa); S_y is the yield strength of the material (MPa); FoS is the factor of safety (no unit).
δmax is the largest linear deflection (mm); δallow is its permitted limit (mm); θmax is the largest angle of twist (rad); θallow is its permitted limit (rad).

blocks.text: A part can pass the strength check and still fail in service. A long shaft may be strong in torsion but twist too much, so a gear on it loses alignment. A slender beam may carry its load without yielding but sag enough to spoil a cutting tool or open a clearance.

The checks use different section properties. Bending strength depends on section modulus Z = I/c; bending stiffness depends on second moment I. Torsion strength depends on polar modulus J/r; torsional stiffness depends on J. A shape can be strong but flexible, or stiff but heavy.
For a straight bar under axial load P, the extension is δ = PL/(AE).

blocks.where: P is the axial load (N); L is the bar length (mm); A is the cross-sectional area (mm²); E is Young's modulus (N/mm² or MPa).

blocks.text: For a circular shaft under torque T, the angle of twist is θ = TL/(GJ).

blocks.where: T is the torque (N·mm); L is the shaft length (mm); G is the shear modulus (N/mm²); J is the polar second moment of area (mm⁴).

blocks.text: For bending, use the standard beam formula that matches the support and load.

sections.h3: Design loop: trial, strength, stiffness, resize

blocks.text: Start with a trial section from standard sizes. Check strength first because a failed strength check means the part is unsafe, not merely inaccurate.

items: Choose a material and its allowable stress, S_y/FoS.
Choose a trial section: width, depth, diameter or standard profile.
Compute the maximum stress from the loads.
Compare σmax with the allowable stress.
Compute the maximum deflection or twist.
Compare δmax with δallow, or θmax with θallow.
If either check fails, resize and repeat. Strength usually needs more Z or J/r; stiffness usually needs more I or J.

blocks.text: Stiffness often controls long shafts and slender beams because deflection grows with length cubed in bending. Strength controls short, heavily loaded parts. The final design must pass both checks, not the easier one.

figure.caption: A trial section is checked first for strength and then for stiffness. Failure at either check sends the designer back to resize; only passing both accepts the part.

spec.aria: A trial section passes a strength check and then a stiffness check; either failure sends the designer back to resize.

examples.question: A simply supported steel beam of span 1.2 m carries a central load of 10 kN. The allowable bending stress is 120 MPa, the allowable deflection is 3 mm, and E = 200 GPa. The section is rectangular with depth h = 2b. Choose the smallest width b that satisfies both checks.
steps: Data: P = 10 kN = 10000 N; L = 1.2 m = 1200 mm; σallow = 120 MPa; δallow = 3 mm; E = 200 GPa = 200000 N/mm²; h = 2b.
Maximum bending moment: M = P L / 4 = 10000 × 1200 / 4 = 3.0 × 10⁶ N·mm.
Section properties: I = b h³ / 12 = (2/3)b⁴; Z = I / (h/2) = (2/3)b³.
Strength check: σ = M / Z = 3.0 × 10⁶ / ((2/3)b³) = 4.5 × 10⁶ / b³ ≤ 120. So b³ ≥ 37500, giving b ≥ 33.47 mm.
Stiffness check: δ = P L³ / (48 E I) = 2.70 × 10⁶ / b⁴ ≤ 3. So b⁴ ≥ 900000, giving b ≥ 30.80 mm.
Strength needs the larger b. Choose b = 33.47 mm; in practice use 34 mm.
Check deflection at b = 33.47 mm: δ = 2.15 mm, which is below 3 mm. Depth h = 2b = 66.94 mm.
examples.answer: The smallest width is b ≈ 33.47 mm, set by strength; use 34 mm, and the deflection is then 2.15 mm, within the 3 mm limit.
examples.check:
P=10000
L=1200
M=P*L/4
sigma=120
Z_req=M/sigma
b_strength=(1.5*Z_req)**(1/3)
E=200000
delta_allow=3
b_stiff=(P*L**3/(48*E*delta_allow*(2/3)))**0.25
b_req=max(b_strength,b_stiff)
I=(2/3)*b_req**4
delta=P*L**3/(48*E*I)
print(f"{b_strength:.2f}")
print(f"{b_stiff:.2f}")
print(f"{b_req:.2f}")
print(f"{delta:.2f}")

traps: Checking strength only. A part can be strong enough and still fail because deflection or twist exceeds the limit.
Using the same section property for both checks. Strength uses Z or J/r; stiffness uses I or J.
Mixing units: kN with mm, GPa with N/mm², or m with mm. Convert to N and mm before substituting.
In torsion, using J/r where J belongs. Twist uses GJ in the denominator, not GJ/r.
Forgetting the factor of safety in the strength check, or comparing working stress with ultimate strength instead of allowable stress.

quiz.q: State the strength check and the stiffness check for a machine part.
quiz.a: Strength: σmax ≤ S_y/FoS. Stiffness: δmax ≤ δallow, and for twist θmax ≤ θallow.

quiz.q: Why can a part pass the strength check and fail the stiffness check?
quiz.a: Strength depends on stress, which depends on load and section modulus. Stiffness depends on deformation, which grows with length and depends on I or J. A long slender part can carry stress safely but deflect too much.

quiz.q: A tie bar of length 500 mm and area 100 mm² carries 20 kN. E = 200 GPa. Find its extension.
A cantilever carries the same end load, and its length is doubled. What happens to its end deflection?
quiz.a: For an end point load, δ = PL³/(3EI). Doubling L multiplies deflection by 2³ = 8.

quiz.q: Which section property controls bending strength and which controls bending stiffness?
quiz.a: Bending strength depends on section modulus Z = I/c. Bending stiffness depends on second moment of area I.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam has P = 8 kN, L = 1 m, E = 200 GPa, I = 2 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Find the central deflection.
A designer increases only the depth of a rectangular beam. Which check benefits more, strength or stiffness?
quiz.a: Both improve, but stiffness improves more. For a rectangle, Z ∝ h² and I ∝ h³, so depth raises I faster than Z.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, stiffness limits often come from precision, clearance, vibration or alignment, not from strength alone. Finite element analysis computes deflection fields for complex parts, and optimisation routines resize sections until strength and stiffness constraints meet. Standards and company design guides give allowable deflections for shafts, beams and frames. Search for deflection-limited design, stiffness sizing, and beam deflection tables.
